answer: Mostly the money is spent in the United States, on American-made weapons. Under the earlier agreement Israel could spend 26.3 percent of the yearly grant at home; the 2016 agreement ends that by fiscal 2028. For fiscal 2025, $450 million of $3.3 billion was set aside for that: roughly 14 percent by our arithmetic. The US co-developed David's Sling and Arrow. US law allows arms sales only for purposes such as legitimate self-defence. A May 2024 State Department report found it reasonable to assess that US arms were used in ways inconsistent with humanitarian law, and Israel's assurances credible. Senate votes to block sales failed, with 18 yes votes in November 2024, 15 in April 2025, and 36 and 40 in April 2026. Opinion is shifting: Gallup finds 65 percent of Democrats side more with Palestinians, and a third of Americans say the US gives Israel too much military aid.

could_not_verify: A source from outside advocacy that says the US gets intelligence from Israel in exchange for the aid: only advocacy writers (AJC, JNS) claim it, so it is not stated as a fact.

An audited figure for the share of aid dollars spent in the United States: no source gives one. The 14 percent in the answer is our arithmetic (450.3 divided by 3,300 million), counts only off-shore procurement, and is not fuel or other items.
How much of the missile defence money is spent in the US each year: the Missile Defense Agency estimate is quoted from the CRS report only.
Three reliable sources for facts 2 and 3 (amounts spent in Israel; where grants go): the law and the CRS are government or primary; the CFR is the only independent reference.
Three reliable sources for fact 4 (joint development) and fact 5 (US law): only two independent sites each.

The text of National Security Memorandum 20 and the State Department's May 2024 report: the White House and State Department pages would not load, so both are described through the CRS, Lawfare, Just Security and Al Jazeera.

Three reliable sources for facts 8 and 9 (polls): the poll owners (Gallup, Pew) plus one news or think-tank report each. Pew's party-by-age breakdown of the military-aid question and Gallup's Republicans-by-age figures were not read.

Whether National Security Memorandum 20 is still in force: the CRS report cited on this card says that on 21 February 2025, according to the Washington Post, the national security adviser rescinded it. Fact 5 describes it as issued in February 2024 and does not say so; the answer says only what the May 2024 report said.
not_claimed: This card does not say the aid should continue, or end.
It does not say Israel has broken US law: the State Department said in 2024 that it had not assessed Israel to be in violation, and the May 2024 report did not reach legal findings.
It does not say Israel gives the US intelligence in return for the aid; that is claimed by advocates and not verified here.
It does not say American opinion decides policy; it reports polls only.

answer_claims.says: Mostly the money is spent in the United States, on American-made weapons.
Under the earlier agreement Israel could spend 26.3 percent of the yearly grant at home; the 2016 agreement ends that by fiscal 2028.
For fiscal 2025, $450 million of $3.3 billion was set aside for that: roughly 14 percent by our arithmetic.
The US co-developed David's Sling and Arrow.
US law allows arms sales only for purposes such as legitimate self-defence.
A May 2024 State Department report found it reasonable to assess that US arms were used in ways inconsistent with humanitarian law, and Israel's assurances credible.
Senate votes to block sales failed, with 18 yes votes in November 2024, 15 in April 2025, and 36 and 40 in April 2026.
Opinion is shifting: Gallup finds 65 percent of Democrats side more with Palestinians, and a third of Americans say the US gives Israel too much military aid.

skeptic.notes: Round 1. Quotes are on their pages and in context. Percentage recomputed: 450.3 / 3,300 = 13.6 percent, 'about 14' is fair; the card now says 'our own arithmetic' in fact 1 as well as the answer, with the $3.3bn base named (CRS, P.L. 119-4), and the $769.3m/$3.5bn = 22 percent figure for the supplemental is shown the same way. Both are appropriated amounts; the 26.3 percent is a ceiling, not a measured spend. Must-fix found: fact 0 said the 26.3 percent was 'under the 2016 agreement'; the White House page says it was the earlier ('current', in 2016) MOU that allowed it, and the 2016 one phases it out (text fixed). Must-fix for the writer: the card describes NSM-20 (Feb 2024) but its own CRS source says it was rescinded 21 Feb 2025; the fact and the card are silent (needs the fact reworded with a source; recorded in could_not_verify). Strongest objection from critics: 'mostly spent in the US' says nothing about whether the aid funds the war; the card answers where, not whether (contested says so, fine). From the pro-aid side: AJC's 'almost all of it is spent in the U.S.' sits in contested as advocacy; CRS's own figures (about 14 to 22 percent in Israel) do not support 'almost all' only as an annual ceiling. Pew's 35 percent 'unsure' and 8 percent 'not enough' are not on the card; the third is 'too much', fair but not the whole picture (should-fix). Senate votes are motions to discharge (and two 2025 resolutions), not final passage votes; 15 yes in April 2025 matches CRS 15-83 and 15-82 and JTA 82-15. Lawfare relabelled reference to news. Only facts 4 (partly), 6, 7 and 8 reach three reliable sources; facts 0 to 3 and 5 do not, so the card stays draft.

citer.notes: Removed: 'but sales went on' (no fact says sales continued; the CRS says NSM-20 assurances were judged 'credible and reliable so as to allow' sales to continue, which fact 5 now carries as 'calling Israel's assurances credible and reliable'), 'Until recently' and 'that share shrinks each year' (fact 0 says phased out, ending in fiscal 2028), '15 to 19 yes votes' (the card carries 18, 15, 36 and 40; 'fewer than 20' is on the Al Jazeera page but not in a fact), and 'up to 40' (stated as the two votes). Reworded the opinion sentence from the single largest Pew figure (42 percent of under-30s) to the whole-population figure plus the Gallup finding, tied to facts 7 and 8. Also dropped 'with Israel' from the co-development sentence (fact 3 says the US developed them jointly; Iron Dome was Israeli) and shortened others to fit the 150-word limit.
